title: The Hardest Word
subject: English
unit: Spring 2: The Tempest (Shakespeare): transformation through forgiveness
source: Written for english/y7 lesson 34 ('The Hardest Word' (teacher-written discussion article, pupil PDF))
intro: Lesson 34: Non-fiction: should we always forgive?. Read the whole text, then annotate it: underline the writer's methods and note their effect in the margin.

passage.title: The Hardest Word
paras: Forgiveness is often praised, but is it always right? Supporters argue that forgiving frees the victim: resentment, they say, is a weight that only the forgiver can put down. Families and friendships survive because people pardon each other's mistakes.
Yet others warn that forgiving too quickly can excuse wrongdoing. If an offender is not sorry, forgiveness may simply invite the harm again. Justice, they insist, must come first.

Both sides have a point. Imagine a friend who borrows your bike and returns it scratched. If they apologise and offer to repair it, forgiving them seems easy and right. But imagine someone who keeps taking things and laughs when you complain. Forgiving them without a word may teach them only that they will never face consequences.

Many faiths and traditions treat forgiveness as a great virtue while still upholding justice. In Islam, a person who has been wronged has the right to fair redress, yet forgiving is praised as the better and nobler choice when it is possible. Forgiveness, in this view, is not pretending that nothing happened; it is choosing not to hold on to revenge.
Perhaps the answer lies between the two: forgiveness is strongest when the truth is faced and the wrong is put right.

questions.q: What is the writer's main viewpoint?
questions.a: Balanced: forgiveness is strongest when the truth is faced and the wrong is put right.

questions.q: Find two methods the writer uses and explain the effect of each.
questions.a: Contrasting viewpoints ('Supporters argue... Yet others warn'); the metaphor of resentment as 'a weight'; the everyday example of the borrowed bike.

questions.q: How does the final paragraph end the argument?
questions.a: It offers a middle way, judging both sides fairly.

questions.q: Write the 'against' side in one sentence using 'However'.
questions.a: However, forgiving too quickly can excuse wrongdoing and invite the harm again.

questions.q: What judgement does the writer reach?
questions.a: Forgiveness is strongest when the truth is faced and the wrong is put right.

questions.q: Core: in the portal response box, write a balanced paragraph: 'Should Prospero forgive his enemies?' Starter: 'Some would argue that Prospero should forgive because... However...'
questions.a: A balanced paragraph: for (breaks the cycle, peace), against (Antonio is not sorry), and a justified judgement.

questions.q: Extend: add an example from life or another text.
questions.a: For example: Stanley in Holes, or a family quarrel that was mended.

questions.q: Stretch: is forgiveness possible without an apology?
questions.a: Answers vary, e.g. yes: forgiveness can free the forgiver even if the other is not sorry.

options: It gives both sides before judging
questions.a: A) It gives both sides before judging. Balance means fair weight to both views; B is one-sided; C is not the defining feature.

questions.q: Answer the ponder in one sentence.
questions.a: No: forgiving means letting go of revenge, not pretending the wrong was acceptable.
